title: Impact of climate change on the suitable niches of an ornithophilous neotropical orchid (Elleanthus brasiliensis) and its pollen vectors
abstract: There is no doubt that climate change not only affects the spatial distribution of organisms but also alters ecological interactions that are crucial for the maintenance and functioning of ecosystems. Much research has been devoted to assessing the impact of global warming on animal-mediated pollination, which is vital for the reproduction of vascular plants. Most analyses have focused on insect pollen vectors, as these are the most common animals involved in pollination. The aim of this study was to investigate the impact of climate change on the distribution of suitable niches of the tropical orchid (Elleanthus brasiliensis) and four hummingbirds reported to serve as pollen vectors for this species (Thalurania glaucopis, Phaethornis pretrei, Phaethornis squalidus, Ramphodon naevius), as well as to estimate the locations of climatic refugia where both orchid and pollinator will co-occur in the future. All species studied will lose suitable niches in different Brazilian biomes as a result of global warming. In the reduced, fragmented potential range of E. brasiliensis, not all orchid populations will have a chance of cross-pollination. Of the birds included in the study, T. glaucopis will be the most important orchid pollinator, being available for basically all of the plant populations. The most endangered populations of E. brasiliensis are located in the southern part of the orchid range where no pollen vectors except of T. glaucopis are predicted to occur in the future. The partial lack of pollen vectors and the fragmentation of geographical ranges will pose serious threats to the long-term survival of the studied orchid. The areas identified in this study as suitable for the occurrence of both the orchid and its pollinator(s) should be considered as climatic refugia and receive additional attention when planning conservation activities.
problem: While numerous studies have focused on climate change's impact on insect-pollinated plants, little is known about threats to bird-pollinated species, specifically the potential for a spatial mismatch between ornithophilous plants and their hummingbird pollinators as their suitable climate niches shift.
method: This study uses maximum entropy modeling to assess the impact of climate change on the distribution of suitable niches for the tropical orchid *Elleanthus brasiliensis* and its four hummingbird pollinators, and to estimate the locations of future climatic refugia where they will co-occur.
task: The task is to investigate the impact of climate change on the distribution of suitable niches for the neotropical orchid *Elleanthus brasiliensis* and its four hummingbird pollinators, and to estimate future locations where both the orchid and its pollinators will co-occur.

innovation: This paper presents the first study assessing the impact of climate change on the spatial availability of hummingbird pollen vectors for a Neotropical orchid species, identifying future climatic refugia and potential spatial mismatches between the orchid and its pollinators.

The future extent of the orchid and hummingbirds suitable niches for 2080– 2100 was predicted using four projections for three Shared Socio-economic Pathways (SSPs) describing alternative pathways of future socio-economic development - SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5 and SSP5–8.5. These storylines differ in predicted greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, expected level of radiative forcing and anticipated achievement of sustainable development goals 59. The SSP1-2.6 scenario assumes CO2 emissions cut to net zero around 2075. In SSP2-4.5 with intermediate GHG emissions consider continuation of CO2 emissions at current levels until 2050. Finally, SSP5–8.5 is based on assumption of high CO2 emissions which triple by 2075. The estimated climate warming in 2080-2100 in analysed scenarios vary from 1.3-2.4°C (SSP1-2.6) to 3.3-5.7°C (SSP5–8.5) 59, In this study projections developed by the Max Planck Institute Earth System Model (MPI-ESM1.2) for the High-Resolution Model Intercomparison Project (HighResMIP) 60 were used, as this forecast is the most reliable within the analyzed geographical area 61.
